intro: In November 1863 the most admired speaker in America talked for two hours at Gettysburg, and the president who followed him spoke for about two minutes. One speech is a footnote. The other is carved in marble. Sixty-six years earlier, an Irish clergyman had calmly proposed that the poor sell their babies as food, and readers who understood him went cold with shame. And this week, somewhere near you, a poster, a column and a four-minute speech all argued the same claim, and the one with the least evidence changed the most minds. Words move people. This unit is about how.

You will start with rhetoric, the old art of choosing words to persuade: the three appeals of trust, feeling and reason; the situation every speech lives in; the devices of repetition, parallelism, antithesis and the question that answers itself. You will read Lincoln, Douglass, Sojourner Truth and the Declaration of Independence as arguments built by people who knew exactly what they were doing. Then you will study tone and voice, from Swift's straight-faced horror to Twain's deadpan, and learn how a reader hears the difference between what a text says and what its writer means. Finally you will take those tools into the world: ads, editorials, speeches and your own feed, where the same moves appear with less honesty and more speed.

By the end you will be able to name what a speaker is doing to you while it is happening, judge whether an argument has earned its conclusion, spot the five most common ways reasoning goes wrong, and write an argument that states the other side's best point and survives it. None of this is about being suspicious of everything. It is about being moved by the right things, for reasons you can explain.
bigQuestion: How do words move people, and how do you tell an argument that has earned your agreement from one that has only won it?

timeline.t: Aristotle sorts persuasion into three appeals: the speaker's character, the audience's feeling, and reason.
Jonathan Swift publishes A Modest Proposal, a calm essay whose monstrous plan exposes how Ireland's poor were treated.
Patrick Henry urges the Virginia Convention to arm; the speech survives only as later listeners remembered it.
The Declaration of Independence sets out a principle, a list of grievances and a conclusion: an argument with a shape.
Sojourner Truth argues for women's rights at Akron from her own labor; her words survive in versions that disagree.
Frederick Douglass asks a Rochester audience what the Fourth of July means to the enslaved.
Lincoln and Douglas debate seven times across Illinois in a strict format that makes dodging expensive.
Lincoln speaks for about two minutes at Gettysburg; Edward Everett's two-hour address is forgotten.
Lincoln's Second Inaugural ends with malice toward none and charity for all as the war closes.
Mark Twain's Advice to Youth mocks the empty way adults lecture the young, in the voice of a solemn adviser.
The same appeals and fallacies fill a feed sorted by feeling, and a reader with the tools can still tell them apart.

words.d: the art of using language to persuade or move an audience
an appeal based on the speaker's character, credibility or shared values
an appeal to the audience's emotions
an appeal to reason through claims, evidence and logical connections
the speaker, audience, purpose and occasion that shape a piece of persuasion
placing two opposite ideas side by side in matched grammatical form
the writer's attitude toward the subject or reader, as shown by the words
a writer's or speaker's choice of words
saying one thing while meaning the opposite
writing that uses irony, exaggeration and mockery to expose a real fault
a pattern of reasoning that looks like an argument but fails to prove its point
the strongest opposing point, stated fairly within your own argument

test.q: A speaker begins by describing her twenty years as a nurse in the neighborhood. Which appeal is she building?
test.why: Her experience makes her credible; credibility and character are ethos.

test.q: Which sentence relies mainly on pathos?
choices: The bridge has failed two inspections.
As an engineer, I have seen this before.
Picture your daughter's school bus on that bridge tomorrow morning.
test.why: A concrete, frightening image aimed at the listener's feelings is pathos.

test.q: What are the four parts of the rhetorical situation?
test.why: Who is speaking, to whom, why, and when frame every act of persuasion.

test.q: Government of the people, by the people, for the people is an example of which device?
test.why: Three phrases built on the same grammatical shape are parallelism.

test.q: Why did Douglass say your Fourth of July instead of our?
choices: To separate himself from listeners who thought he was one of them
Because he was not an American citizen
Because the speech was written for a British audience
Because he had forgotten the date
test.why: The pronoun choice, diction, builds a wall between the speaker and the audience on purpose.

test.q: What does a rhetorical analysis explain?
choices: How the text tries to move its audience
test.why: Analysis is about method, not agreement.

test.q: Swift's calm tone in A Modest Proposal produces horror in the reader. What does this show?
choices: Swift did not understand his own essay
Tone and mood can pull apart on purpose
test.why: Tone is the writer's attitude; mood is the reader's feeling; Swift set them against each other deliberately.

test.q: Replacing the animal was removed with they dragged the poor old dog out changes the tone through what?
test.why: The words changed, and their connotations changed the tone. That is diction.

test.q: A fire station burns down. Which kind of irony is this?
test.why: Situational irony is when what happens is the opposite of what was expected.

test.q: What does satire always have that a mere joke does not?
choices: A real target and a purpose
test.why: Satire aims its laughter at a real fault in order to expose it.

test.q: A student writes yo whats due to a teacher. What kind of mistake is this?
test.why: The level of formality did not fit the situation.

test.q: Which of these is the best evidence for a claim about all students in a district?
choices: A story about the writer's cousin
A survey of the writer's five friends
A study from 1985 of a different state
A district-wide survey of 2,000 students from last year
test.why: It is large, recent, from a relevant source and directly about the group in the claim.

test.q: So you want to let students sleep until noon? in reply to a request for an 8:30 start is which fallacy?
test.why: It answers a weaker claim that nobody made.

test.q: Why does a social media feed tend to fill with weak arguments?
choices: Because users are not allowed to cite evidence
Because the form rewards short, certain, emotional claims
Because posts are reviewed by editors
test.why: The rhetorical situation of a feed favors what travels fastest, and that is rarely careful reasoning.

test.q: What should an argument do with the strongest point on the other side?
choices: Leave it out so readers do not think of it
Mention it briefly in the last sentence
Restate it in a weaker form and attack that
State it fairly as a counterclaim and answer it
test.why: A counterclaim in its strongest form, followed by an honest rebuttal, is what makes an argument survive.

write.prompt: Choose one text from this unit: the Gettysburg Address, Douglass's Fourth of July speech, A Modest Proposal, or the three start-time texts from Chapter 39. Make a claim about which single choice, of structure, diction, tone or evidence, does the most to move its audience, and prove it.
tips: State your claim in one exact sentence that names the choice and its effect, not just that the text uses ethos, pathos and logos.
Quote the actual words that show the choice, briefly, and look closely at them; do not summarize the whole text.
Explain your reasoning: how does this choice fit the rhetorical situation, the speaker, audience, purpose and occasion?
State the strongest case for a different choice as your counterclaim, and answer it honestly or narrow your claim.
Check your own argument for the fallacies from Chapter 39 before you hand it in.
